title: THE WOMAN JESUS PRAISED WITHOUT EVER NAMING HER
paragraphs: THE WOMAN JESUS PRAISED WITHOUT EVER NAMING HER
She walked into the story carrying a scandal. She walked out carrying words from Jesus that would follow the Gospel across the world.
There is something almost painful about the way Scripture introduces her.
No name.
No respectable family history.
No religious title.
No carefully polished testimony explaining how she arrived at this moment.
Matthew and Mark preserve her story, but neither tells us what her mother called her when she was a child.
Jesus knew her name.
History simply wasn't given it.
And somehow, that makes what happened even more powerful.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to believe nobody really sees you.
Perhaps people remember what happened to you but forget who you are.
Perhaps your mistakes have been repeated more often than your repentance.
Perhaps you have spent years quietly serving Jesus while louder Christians received the recognition.
Perhaps nobody applauded the nights you resisted temptation.
Nobody saw you close the door and cry.
Nobody knew how difficult it was for you to pray again after disappointment.
Nobody understood what it cost you just to keep believing.
Then you need to meet the unnamed woman Jesus refused to forget.
Her story appears shortly before the crucifixion.
Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, when a woman approached Him carrying an alabaster flask containing extraordinarily valuable perfume.
Matthew tells us:
“And when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, there came unto him a woman having an alabaster box of very precious ointment, and poured it on his head, as he sat at meat.”
— Matthew 26:6–7, KJV
Mark gives us another striking detail.
The perfume was nardou pistikēs polytelous — νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτελοῦς — costly pure nard.
Then she did something irreversible.
Mark says she broke the alabaster container.
She didn't merely loosen the lid.
She broke it.
And she poured the perfume over Jesus.
Immediately, the fragrance filled a room that was about to become a courtroom.
Because devotion is not always admired by people who witness it.
Sometimes it is interrogated.
Some of those present became indignant.
“What a waste.”
That is essentially their accusation.
Mark records:
“Why was this waste of the ointment made?”
— Mark 14:4, KJV
Imagine hearing those words while your offering is still running down the head of Jesus.
Waste.
Perhaps that word has been spoken over something precious in your life too.
You wasted your youth.
You wasted that opportunity.
You wasted those years.
You wasted your money.
You wasted your love.
You wasted your life.
Or perhaps people have looked at what you surrendered to Christ and considered that waste too.
Why take your faith so seriously?
Why forgive them?
Why remain sexually pure?
Why give?
Why serve?
Why pray when nobody is watching?
Why refuse the compromise everybody else accepts?
Why pour so much of yourself into Jesus?
And somewhere beneath those questions is the ancient accusation:
Why this waste?
But Jesus heard them.
And then He defended her.
“Let her alone.”
Those words matter.
The woman does not appear to defend herself.
Jesus does it for her.
Then He says something astonishing:
“She hath wrought a good work on me.”
— Mark 14:6, KJV
The Greek is beautiful:
καλὸν ἔργον ἠργάσατο ἐν ἐμοί
kalon ergon ērgasato en emoi.
She has done a beautiful — noble, good — work toward Me.
The room called it waste.
Jesus called it beautiful.
Do not move past that too quickly.
Because sometimes the difference between shame and freedom is discovering that Jesus does not describe you the way the crowd does.
People may reduce you to your worst chapter.
Jesus sees what grace is writing next.
People may remember your failure.
Jesus sees your faith.
People may measure your offering by its market value.
Jesus sees the love behind the breaking.
People may ask what you have accomplished.
Jesus may be looking at what you surrendered.
And then Jesus says something even more remarkable.
“She hath done what she could.”
— Mark 14:8, KJV
Read that again.
She did what she could.
Not what Peter could.
Not what John could.
Not what somebody richer, stronger, more educated, more respected, more articulate, or more influential could.
What she could.
There are people destroying themselves because they believe Jesus is disappointed that they cannot give Him somebody else's life.
You look at another Christian's ministry and feel insignificant.
You see someone else's family and feel behind.
You see someone else's testimony and wonder why yours is still messy.
You see someone else's spiritual discipline and feel ashamed.
You see someone else's platform and wonder whether God notices your tiny corner of obedience.
But perhaps Jesus is not asking you to become them.
Perhaps He is asking whether you will place what is actually in your hands at His feet.
She did what she could.
And apparently, to Jesus, that was beautiful.
But there is something deeper happening in Bethany.
Jesus says:
“She is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.”
— Mark 14:8, KJV
The cross is approaching.
The disciples have heard Jesus speak about His death, yet again and again they struggle to comprehend what He means.
And here stands this unnamed woman pouring expensive perfume over the One who is going to die.
Whether she understood every theological implication of her act, Jesus Himself interpreted it in relation to His burial.
The fragrance was pointing toward a tomb.
That changes everything.
This is not merely a touching story about generosity.
It stands beneath the shadow of Calvary.
Jesus Christ came to give Himself for sinners.
The Son of God was moving toward betrayal, condemnation, crucifixion, death, burial, and resurrection.
The woman broke her alabaster vessel.
Soon Christ's body would be given.
She poured out something precious.
Soon His blood would be poured out.
She gave extravagantly.
Soon He would give infinitely more.
Her perfume was expensive.
His sacrifice was beyond price.
And suddenly her offering doesn't look extravagant anymore.
It looks like a response.
Because that is Christianity.
We do not sacrifice in order to convince God to love us.
We surrender because in Christ we discover how profoundly He already has.
“We love him, because he first loved us.”
— 1 John 4:19, KJV
The Gospel does not begin with your gift to Jesus.
It begins with Jesus giving Himself for you.
That is why the center of this story cannot ultimately be the woman.
The center must remain Christ.
She is unforgettable because of the One upon whom she poured the perfume.
And then Jesus gives her something she never asked for.
A memorial.
“Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her.”
— Mark 14:9, KJV
The Greek word translated “memorial” is μνημόσυνον — mnēmosynon.
A remembrance.
A memorial.
Something by which a person or deed is remembered.
Do you see the holy irony?
Scripture doesn't give us her name here.
Yet Jesus made sure her act would not disappear.
The world may not know what to call her.
But the Gospel remembers what she did.
And approximately two thousand years later, here you are.
Reading about her.
Jesus' words came true.
Kings disappeared.
Empires collapsed.
Generations died.
Languages changed.
Cities became ruins.
Yet a woman in Bethany broke an alabaster vessel over Jesus...
and we are still talking about it.
That should make every hidden believer tremble with hope.
Because heaven's definition of significance is radically different from ours.
We live in an age obsessed with being known.
Followers.
Views.
Reach.
Recognition.
Verification.
Platforms.
Names.
Images.
Brands.
But one of the most famous acts of devotion in the Gospel narratives was performed by a woman Matthew and Mark never name.
Maybe obscurity isn't the tragedy we think it is.
Maybe being unknown by the world is bearable when you are fully known by Christ.
Maybe your greatest spiritual legacy will not be your name.
Maybe it will be the fragrance your obedience leaves behind.
But there is another uncomfortable detail in Mark's account.
Immediately after Jesus declares that this woman's act will be remembered wherever the Gospel is proclaimed, Mark tells us:
“And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went unto the chief priests, to betray him unto them.”
— Mark 14:10, KJV
Feel the contrast.
One person is pouring something precious upon Jesus.
Another is preparing to hand Jesus over.
One moves toward surrender.
The other toward betrayal.
One considers Jesus worth the cost.
The other begins negotiating.
And suddenly the story stops being safely historical.
Because every heart must answer the question hidden inside that room:
What is Jesus worth to me?
Not what do I say He is worth on Sunday.
Not what worship song makes me emotional.
Not what Bible verse appears in my biography.
What is He worth when following Him costs something?
When repentance means deleting something.
Ending something.
Confessing something.
Forgiving someone.
Walking away from an ungodly relationship.
Returning what isn't yours.
Breaking with secret sin.
Choosing integrity when dishonesty would be profitable.
Saying no when your flesh is screaming yes.
Trusting Christ when obedience makes you look foolish.
What happens when your alabaster jar finally has to break?
Because many of us want Jesus...
without breaking the jar.
We want salvation without surrender.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
Grace without transformation.
A Savior who rescues us from hell but never interferes with our idols.
But biblical grace does not merely pardon.
Grace transforms.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could become comfortable prisoners of the sins He came to save us from.
He calls sinners to Himself.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He makes new.
And perhaps this is where the unnamed woman finds you.
Maybe your alabaster jar is not perfume.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe it is pornography nobody knows about.
Maybe it is bitterness you have justified for ten years.
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is your obsession with approval.
Maybe it is resentment toward God because your prayers were not answered the way you wanted.
Maybe it is the secret identity you protect because you are terrified of what would happen if somebody knew the truth.
Maybe you have mastered Christian vocabulary while your heart has slowly become cold.
You still say “God bless.”
You still share verses.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
But somewhere inside, the fragrance disappeared.
And Jesus is calling you back.
Not to religious performance.
To Himself.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Because the Gospel has never depended upon pretending your story is clean.
The Gospel announces that Christ came precisely because sinners are not.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23, KJV
And yet Scripture continues:
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
— Romans 3:24, KJV
That word “freely” comes from the Greek δωρεάν — dōrean — freely, as a gift.
Grace cannot be purchased with perfume.
It cannot be purchased with money.
It cannot be purchased with religious activity.
Jesus purchased redemption.
That distinction matters.
Supporting Gospel work can be an act of gratitude, stewardship, generosity, and partnership in proclaiming truth.
But Christ alone saves.
So if this story is exposing something in you, do not merely become emotional.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Confess.
Believe.
Bring Him the hidden thing.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the years you think you wasted.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are exhausted from pretending to be.
The cross is sufficient.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is alive.
And He is still rewriting stories.
Maybe that is why you needed the woman without a name.
Because perhaps you have been waiting for recognition when what your soul actually needed was surrender.
Perhaps you wanted everybody to understand your story.
Jesus wanted your heart.
Perhaps you wanted people to defend you.
Jesus wanted you to discover that His verdict matters more.
Perhaps you wanted your name remembered.
Jesus wanted His name written across your life.
That is the transformation.
From hiding to confession.
From bondage to freedom.
From performing to surrendering.
From being consumed with your reputation to becoming consumed with Christ.
And if you are reading this with tears gathering in your eyes because something hidden has finally been touched, don't rush away from that conviction.
Be honest.
And if grace has already begun rebuilding what sin, trauma, failure, or shame tried to destroy, testify:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Your comment does not save you.
Jesus does.
But sometimes confession breaks the isolation in which darkness grows, and sometimes another struggling believer needs to see that they are not the only person still fighting.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not twenty random names.
One.
The friend quietly drifting from Jesus.
The son who stopped going to church.
The daughter carrying shame.
The husband fighting secretly.
The wife who feels spiritually exhausted.
The believer who thinks God is finished with them.
The unbeliever who assumes Christianity is merely religion for people pretending to have perfect lives.
A share cannot save a soul.
But it can carry words about the Savior to a person who desperately needs to hear them.

And if you believe Gospel-centered truth deserves to travel farther than gossip, outrage, temptation, and empty entertainment, helping distribute Scripture-centered content is one practical way to use your influence for God's glory.
There may come a night when you are the person who needs to remember:
The room called it waste.
Jesus called it beautiful.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Christ, consider following the page and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well.

We want this community to remain a place where Scripture is opened, sin is confronted, wounded people are pointed toward Christ, believers are strengthened, and the Gospel remains more important than the platform carrying it.
It does not make you more saved.
It does not replace giving to your local church, loving your neighbor, feeding the hungry, caring for your family, or obeying Christ in the ordinary places nobody sees.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for the glory of God.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Make Jesus known.
Because somewhere beyond your screen may be another unnamed person.
Someone ashamed.
Someone exhausted.
Someone secretly addicted.
Someone questioning whether God could still want them.
Someone convinced their worst chapter has become their permanent identity.
And perhaps God can use something as ordinary as your share to put the truth of Christ in front of them.
The woman in Bethany probably never imagined people thousands of years later would still be talking about what happened in that room.
She simply brought what she had.
She broke it.
She poured it out.
And Jesus remembered.
So perhaps the question isn't whether the world will remember your name.
Perhaps the question is what your life will say about His.
When your reputation is gone...
when the applause stops...
when your possessions belong to somebody else...
when your social-media accounts disappear...
when nobody remembers how many followers you had...
when your body returns to dust...
what fragrance will remain?
May it be said that you loved Jesus.
That when grace found your scandal, you stopped running.
That when Christ exposed your sin, you repented instead of hiding.
That when the world called obedience foolish, you kept pouring.
That when following Jesus became costly, you discovered that He was worth more than the jar.
And that when people forgot your name...
Jesus knew it.
Here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
You do not need the world to remember your name when your surrendered life carries the fragrance of the Name above every name.
Jesus is still receiving sinners.
Jesus is still forgiving the repentant.
Jesus is still restoring broken people.
Jesus is still worthy of everything we pour at His feet.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories the world thought were already over.
